title: Four entered the orchard (Chagigah 14b)
hook: four sages entered the mystical garden; only Akiva came out whole
carry: enter in peace, leave in peace

segments.voice: Yesterday Honi woke after seventy years to a world that didn't know him. Your line was friendship or death. Did you reach out to an old companion? Day two hundred eighty-seven.

Think of something deep that can go wrong. Deep water. A deep dive into a subject that takes over your life. A retreat that leaves one person calm and another shaken. Depth is wonderful, and it isn't always safe. The Talmud has a short, strange story, just a few lines long, about four great sages who went somewhere very deep. It calls the place pardes, an orchard. Four went in. Only one came out the way he went in. Today, the orchard.
screen: `DEPTH ISN'T ALWAYS SAFE.` → `FOUR SAGES, ONE ORCHARD.` → `ONLY ONE CAME OUT WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Pardes is an old Persian word for a walled garden. Greek borrowed the same word, and English got paradise from it. In tractate Chagigah, the rabbis teach: four entered the pardes. Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Acher, and Rabbi Akiva. Ben Azzai looked, and died. Ben Zoma looked, and was harmed; the tradition understands his mind was shaken. Acher, whose real name was Elisha ben Abuya, cut the shoots, meaning he broke from the tradition entirely; that's why they call him Acher, the other one. And Rabbi Akiva entered in peace, and left in peace. That's the whole story. It never says exactly what the orchard was. Most readers understand it as a deep mystical experience, a kind of journey toward God. Some scholars think it's a picture of dangerous study of the deepest secrets. The sources are simply silent on the details, and the silence seems to be the point. Rabbi Akiva even gave the others a warning: when you reach the stones of pure marble, don't say, water, water. Nobody fully agrees what that means, either. Centuries later, Jewish teachers turned the word into an acronym, P-R-D-S, for four ways of reading the Torah: the plain meaning, the hint, the teaching, and the secret. The orchard became the whole depth of the text. And Akiva's way through it became a model: go in, go deep, and come out whole.
screen: `PARDES: A WALLED GARDEN.` · `FOUR WENT IN.` · `ONLY AKIVA LEFT IN PEACE.` · `THE SOURCES DON'T SAY WHAT IT WAS.` · then, large: `ENTER IN PEACE, LEAVE IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back at this week: my children won, these and these, Beruriah's reading, the jewels on loan, two in the desert, Honi's long sleep, and now the orchard. Settle, and breathe. Enter your two minutes on purpose. Feel your feet, your seat, your breath. Go as deep into stillness as feels right. Near the end, come back on purpose too. Notice your hands. Notice the room. Leave the way you came in: whole. The bell holds the time.
Pardes. An orchard, the root of paradise. Four sages entered; only Rabbi Akiva entered in peace and left in peace.
Your line: enter in peace, leave in peace. Today, whenever you go deep into something, notice how you come back out. Day two hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition has long treated mystical study with caution, and many communities traditionally taught Kabbalah only to mature students; the PaRDeS acronym is widely used to describe levels of reading Torah.

original.note: Hebrew: orchard, a loanword from Persian, related to paradise.

trapdoor: what it means: the depths, of God or of the text, where not everyone comes out whole.
what a scholar hears: the story is in Tosefta Chagigah 2:3 and Chagigah 14b, and PaRDeS as peshat, remez, derash, sod is medieval.

notes: Chagigah 14b paraphrased. 'Ben Zoma was harmed' is often understood as losing his sanity; the script says his mind was shaken.
Pardes: from Old Persian (Avestan pairidaeza), via Greek paradeisos; confirm phrasing.
The PaRDeS acronym is usually traced to the 13th century (Zohar circles, Moses de Leon, Bahya ben Asher); the script says 'centuries later'.
Scholarly views on what the pardes was (mystical ascent vs. esoteric study) are summarized without ranking.
